title: Chain clips from the last frame, and check the join
rule: When a scene runs over several clips, start each clip from the last frame (or a short run of last frames) of the one before and check the join.
why: Models extended chunk by chunk are conditioned on the previous chunk (res-001, res-015); naive continuation without that conditioning makes hard cuts.
how: Pass the previous clip tail as the start picture; flag a step in picture difference at the join.

monofilm.where: public/js/pack.js smoothness (flags a jump inside a returned clip)
monofilm.idea: Compare last frame of clip N with first frame of clip N+1 and flag a step above the clip own median.

title: Keep a fixed anchor picture, not only the previous clip
rule: Condition every clip of a scene on the same approved anchor picture in addition to the previous clip tail.
why: StreamingT2V reuses first-chunk features as a long-term appearance anchor to limit drift; FramePack ablations test drift prevention against pure next-frame chaining.
how: Same hero reference in each clip request; re-anchor rather than chain more than a few clips.

monofilm.where: src/takereview.js (start and end pictures are ground truth for review)
monofilm.idea: Send the scene anchor picture as a reference with every clip, not only the previous tail.

title: Treat extension drift as error accumulation and cap chain length
rule: Cap how many clips are chained from generated tails and restart from a fresh approved picture after the cap.
why: Exposure bias: models trained on clean context degrade when the context is their own output; Self Forcing and Connected Self Forcing exist to reduce this long-horizon drift (res-004, res-005).
how: Re-approve a still every 2 to 3 clips; the paper numbers do not give a safe cap, so tune from review results.

monofilm.idea: Count chained clips per scene and force a fresh keyframe past a configurable cap.

title: Generate all shots of a scene with shared context where the model allows it
rule: If a model supports multi-shot or scene-level context, generate the shots of one scene together rather than as unrelated prompts.
why: LCT lets attention span all shots of a scene to learn scene-level consistency; VGoT keeps identity with portrait tokens and resets at shot boundaries.
how: Prefer a multi-shot mode or shared reference set; otherwise reuse the same references per shot.

monofilm.idea: Expose a multi-shot mode when the model has one.

title: Plan scene text before pictures, with an LLM script stage
rule: Write a scene-by-scene script with characters, places and style first, then derive pictures and clips from it.
why: VideoStudio, MovieAgent, DreamFactory, Anim-Director and MovieDreamer all put an LLM script/storyboard stage ahead of generation; MovieAgent uses a character bank.
how: Keep one character bank and one style line reused by every shot.

monofilm.where: Scene writer and film.pictures in the wizard

title: Generate reference images for recurring entities and reuse them
rule: Create one reference picture per recurring character, place and key object, and condition every clip on it.
why: VideoStudio generates reference images for recurring entities; Phantom, VACE, BindWeave and SkyReels-V3 all take reference images as the consistency mechanism.
how: Neutral pose, plain background, then reuse unchanged.

title: Do not rely on reference conditioning in fast causal modes
rule: Expect weaker reference fidelity in real-time autoregressive generators and re-check identity there.
why: Adapting VACE to a causal, KV-cached model kept 20-30% extra latency but reference-to-video fidelity became severely worse than batch VACE.
how: If a fast mode is used, run the identity review on every take.

monofilm.where: src/takereview.js identity check runs on all takes
monofilm.idea: Raise review strictness when the chosen model is a streaming or distilled variant.

title: Use references from a different scene than the target frame
rule: When training or choosing references, prefer pictures of the subject that differ in pose and setting from the shot being made.
why: Phantom-Data built cross-pair data (reference from another scene) to reduce copy-paste; it kept identity on par with in-pair training while improving prompt alignment.
how: Do not use the first frame of the shot as its own reference.

monofilm.idea: Warn when the reference is a crop of the very shot being prompted.

title: Limit simultaneous subjects and check each one
rule: Keep few characters per clip and check each separately.
why: Phantom targets multi-subject confusion and BindWeave grounds each entity role; the surveys note multi-subject character consistency is still weak.
how: Per-character look check against its reference.

title: Give several views of one subject when 3D consistency matters
rule: Supply more than one reference view (front, side) of a character or object that turns on screen.
why: MV-S2V uses multiple views of one subject for 3D-level consistency and separates views with shifted positional encoding.
how: Front and side sheet; plain background.

monofilm.idea: Allow a second reference view per character in the wizard.

title: Identity needs face-level detail, not only a description
rule: For people, supply a clear face reference; words alone do not hold identity.
why: ConsisID injects low-frequency global face features and high-frequency detail from one face image; MoCA reports over 5% better face similarity with its identity method.
how: Front-facing, even light, face large in frame.

title: Review start and end frames against ground-truth pictures
rule: Judge identity and place against the approved pictures, not the prompt text, and report which frames differ.
why: VBench scores identity consistency as its own dimension; learned judges such as VideoScore correlate with humans at 77.1 Spearman, far above older metrics.
how: Send approved pictures plus sampled frames to the judge.

title: Prefer a learned or VLM judge over plain frame metrics
rule: Use a multimodal judge for review and keep cheap numeric checks only for cuts and freezes.
why: VideoScore reaches 77.1 Spearman with humans, about 50 points above earlier metrics; VBench-2.0 uses VLM/LLM judges for faithfulness; EvalCrafter shows weighting metrics to match people beats a plain average.
how: Numeric: tailHold, smoothness, cuts. Semantic: the judge.

title: Measure physics and counts with targeted checks
rule: Expect physics to fail often and check counts, solid-liquid contact and conservation separately.
why: VideoPhy best model satisfied caption and physics in only 39.6% of videos; VideoPhy-2 best joint score was 22% on hard actions, worst on conservation of mass and momentum; T2V-CompBench finds numeracy hard.
how: Keep actions simple; ask the judge for count and state changes.

title: Do not trust a single benchmark ranking
rule: Pick a video model by testing your own prompts, not by a leaderboard order.
why: Physics-IQ Verified shows a small audit changes ranking (Kendall tau 0.46 over six models); Sci-VBench finds perceptual quality scores tightly clustered while grounding varies widely.
how: Run a fixed internal prompt set per model.

monofilm.idea: Keep a small regression prompt set and score each model on it.

title: Condition on both first and last frame for controlled endings
rule: When a clip must land on a given end state, supply both first and last frame, using a model or sampler built for it.
why: Image-to-video models are built for a start frame; ViBiDSampler and Generative Inbetweening adapt them for two keyframes and the large-motion paper adds a first/last-frame encoder.
how: Make the last picture reachable; huge changes need intermediate keyframes.

monofilm.where: public/js/pack.js tailHold (detects a model reaching the end picture early and holding it)

title: Several keyframes beat one for long motion
rule: For long or large motion, add intermediate keyframes instead of only the first frame.
why: KeyVID conditions on several keyframes; DiffuseSlide notes first-keyframe-only conditioning is too weak for later frames.
how: One keyframe about every few seconds of action.

monofilm.idea: Let the shot list place a mid-clip keyframe picture.

title: Trim a frozen tail instead of keeping it
rule: Cut a clip where it stops moving at the end.
why: Not measured by these papers: Monofilm own observation is that a model given an end picture may reach it early and hold it; the papers only show end-frame conditioning exists.
how: Measure hold at the end; trim, or retry with action spread to the final frame.

title: Penalise hard cuts and jumps inside a single shot
rule: Flag a step in frame difference far above the clip median, and retry.
why: Naive extension makes hard cuts (StreamingT2V); VBench scores motion smoothness and temporal flickering as dimensions.
how: Retry advice: one continuous shot, same place and light.

title: Retry with a new seed and the judge advice, with a ceiling
rule: Retry a flawed take a few times with a changed seed and added advice, then stop and ask a person.
why: Judge agreement with people is imperfect (VideoScore 77.1), and models fail physics most of the time (VideoPhy), so repeated blind retries are costly.
how: Stop after three takes.

title: Self-checking agents: let the pipeline keep the best candidate
rule: Generate candidates and let a checker pick, rather than accept the first output.
why: Anim-Director evaluates its own images and keeps the best; VGoT adds self-validation of storylines.
how: Pick among takes using the judge result.

monofilm.where: retryAdvice and takereview with picked take

title: Break the story into one idea per shot with fixed transitions
rule: Plan shots with explicit transitions and a shot list, not a single long prompt.
why: VGoT expands one sentence into shot descriptions and cinematic specs across five domains and resets at shot boundaries, giving 10x fewer manual adjustments.
how: One action per clip.

title: Use surveys to pick architecture by length target
rule: Choose the generation paradigm from the target length: divide-and-conquer (keyframes then fill) or temporal autoregressive.
why: The long-video survey separates these two paradigms and notes frame skipping and motion inconsistency remain in both; the storytelling survey reports around 150 s with frame redundancy.
how: Short scene: keyframes plus first/last frame; long: chunk chaining with re-anchoring.
